newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia army hawk fired as sop to rebels - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Colombia army hawk fired as sop to rebels - analysts.

text.p: The dismissal of Colombia's hawkish armed forces chief is an overly generous concession to leftist rebels in a bid to start talks to end the country's long-running conflict, military experts say.
President Ernesto Samper, citing "reasons of state," fired Gen. Harold Bedoya on Thursday after a series of disagreements over proposals to launch a fresh peace process.

Bedoya consistently said he would not sit down to "negotiate with criminals" and said Samper's peace plans were tantamount to allowing the guerrillas to ram the "law of the jungle, the law of the most violent" down Colombia's throat.

"We're sacrificing a general with an exemplary career for a peace process that we don't know how or what will be like," ex-defence minister Rafael Pardo said. "This was a questionable decision which could cause aggravation among the armed forces."
Retired Gen. Fernando Landazabal echoed Pardo's comments, saying: "This decision was (due to) pressure from the guerrilla."

After Samper fired Bedoya, he named Gen. Jose Manuel Bonett to replace him. But Bedoya quickly issued a brief statement saying he had not been informed of his firing and that he would not step down voluntarily.

Bedoya's stance generated confusion and irritation in political circles, with some politicians condemning his attitude as an "act of insubordination". But there was no suggestion that the spurned general was preparing a rebellion, in a country where serving military men have had little direct involvement in politics for the last 45 years.
Guerrilla leaders have not directly called for Bedoya's dismissal as a condition for peace talks to start, but they have criticised Samper for letting the military call the political shots.

"Until there is a thorough shake-up of the armed forces and civilian authority is imposed on military authority, it will be very difficult to find any solution to the social and armed conflict in Colombia," Joaquin Gomez, a regional leader of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's largest guerrilla army, told Reuters in a recent interview.

One of the most public clashes between Samper and Bedoya -- appointed armed forces chief just 8-1/2 months ago -- came last month. Bedoya condemned Samper's decision to temporarily demilitarize a huge swathe of southern Colombia to allow FARC rebels to release 70 troops they had been holding prisoner, some for more than nine months.
He dubbed the troop handover, widely covered by the media, as "a circus attended by many clowns" -- a veiled reference to presidential peace envoy, Jose Noe Rios.
The outgoing military chief repeatedly called for a tougher hand against the guerrillas and demanded more equipment and troops to defeat them on the battlefield.

Government ministers, however, have called for more efficient military spending and many believe the army's counterinsurgency efforts have proved unsuccessful in quelling one of the bloodiest guerrilla offensives in three decades of war.

In comments to reporters on Friday, Alvaro Leyva, member of the Catholic Church-backed National Reconciliation Commission, welcomed the firing of Bedoya, describing him as a "stick jammed in the wheel of the peace process".
A recent edition of Voz, the official organ of the Communist Party -- often seen by the military as a political wing of the FARC -- was even more scathing, dubbing Bedoya a "bomb at the peace table".

It is not clear whether the appointment of Bonett, who like Bedoya was trained at the U.S. School of the Americas, will be enough to lure the rebels into the peace process that Samper launched in the wake of the troop handover.

"Bedoya is an inflexible hard man. Whereas Bonett is a flexible hard man. They're both sons of the Cold War but Bonett realises that what was possible in the 1980s is no longer possible in the 1990s," political analyst Eduardo Pizarro told Reuters.

But Pardo doubted Bonett's position on negotiating with the FARC and the smaller Cuban-inspired National Liberation Army (ELN), which has killed at least 30 soldiers so far this month, would be radically different from that of Bedoya.
"In the armed forces there are no personal positions but only institutional positions. It's very naive to think that by removing Bedoya you can change military doctrine," he said.
